chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Washa', who said:
I heard Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) saying: 'The butted one, the fallen one, and what the predator has eaten, when you find its throat intact, slaughter it and eat.'

key_terms.إِذَا أَدْرَكْتَ ذَكَاتَهُ: When you find its throat (or main vessel of slaughter) intact.
key_terms.النَّطِيحَةُ: An animal that died by being butted by the horns of another animal.
key_terms.وَالْمُتَرَدِّيَةُ: An animal that died by falling from a height.
key_terms.وَمَا أَكَلَ السَّبُعُ: What the predator (wild beast) has eaten or killed.

ai.seo_question: How to determine if an animal that died naturally is halal to eat according to Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the Shia juristic distinction between *maytah* (naturally dead) and *dhakih* (ritually slaughtered) by establishing that the integrity of the throat determines permissibility for these three specific modes of death. It reflects the principle that the method of death does not inherently render the meat haram if the primary slaughter vessels remain intact, allowing for ritual slaughter to complete the process. This ruling is central to the Shia methodology of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in determining the status of food.

en.hubeali: Al Husayn Bin Muhammad, from Moala Bin Muhammad, from Al Washa who said,
‘I heard Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> saying: ‘The (animal) butted by the horn, and the one killed by a fall, and what the predators eat, when you come over to it, slaughter it, so eat’.
en.sarwar: 1. Al-Husayn from Muhammad has narrated from Mu‘alla’ ibn Muhammad from af-Washsha’ who has said the foiiowing: “

Abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, would say, ‘If you arrive in time (when it still is alive) to slaughter an animal butted by other animals, fallen from height or eaten by predators, you can use it for food.’”
